en: There is one who girded himself for battle,
A renowned warrior indeed;
I shall seek and find my support,
And muster the army of my father Akun.
Before anyone else, I shall hear
What Kyyaz has to say.
If Kyyaz shows hostility,
I shall have Khan Akun rally his people.
Seeking support in a known land,
Seeking a place to gird myself for battle,
I shall stand firm against distress;
I shall steel my soul
And raise this only child.”
Making a warrior of her woman’s head,
Making a banner of her grieving head,
Moonlike Aichürök
Washed the afterbirth herself,
And cut the cord herself.
Then she laid him in a white shirt
And carefully swaddled him.
You have not held races and children’s games,
Gladdening all who speak of them;
You have given no feast for the people.
Glad tidings, Kyyaz—heed my words!
The trust entrusted to you,
O lionhearted warrior Kyyaz,
I have brought to you myself!
Your broad road has opened wider;
If the child survives and grows,
Your reach will span the world.
Set your thoughts in good order;
Warrior Kyyaz, take and raise your child!”
After Aichürök spoke thus,
Brave Kyyaz burned inwardly,
But said little and made no reply.
He recognized that the child
Was indeed a true calamity.
Realizing it, brave Kyyaz thought,
“Now true suffering has come;
A destined enemy has arrived.
Almighty God the Creator
Has now given me grief.
A child has been found today,
But more than a child, this affliction
Is a black demon of disaster!
My seven sorceress crones—
Without caring what a horse was worth,
I freely gave them my horse;
Without caring what a robe was worth,
I freely gave them my robe.
Those bribed old women
Have proved worthless:
They could not steal the child,
Could not finish him off!
You fawning, rabid curs—
If I do not round you up,
If I do not loose a glorious slaughter
Upon every one of you,
If I do not take your heads by the sword
And drag you along the road—”
Shining like the risen Moon,
Glowing like a bright ornament,
She stepped lightly forward,
Carrying her infant,
Her white breast bared.
Softly she spoke these words;
Her tongue was eloquent, her speech honeyed—
No other soul was like her.
She turned her neck like a young doe;
Aichürök shone as if touched by moonlight.
Your Chürök, daughter of Akun—
Not merely Chürök, but your storm—
Before Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
The resourceful woman Aichürök
Proclaimed the glad tidings:
“Be pleased with my words;
Glad tidings to you, Kyyaz!
Your fortune has filled like a lake,
Your train has grown a fathom long.
Your destiny has truly prospered:
Your moonlike wife Chürök
Has given birth to a son!
Your companion who reads the stars above,
Aichürök, your own consort,
Now stands here to show you
The fulfillment of your mighty hopes,
O warrior Khan Kyyaz—the child is yours.
Hang a talisman around his neck;
Saying, ‘A woman of renown has given birth,’
Raise him, my valiant Kyyaz.
Take the child who has come as your heir
And make him master of the inheritance.
The Seven Valleys are your land,
And the Jediger, who dwell there,
Are your people.
Gather all your people from across the land
And hold a feast of celebration.
You have taken many wives,
Yet never before have you had a child.
Let the road ahead stretch far—
Twisting his face and groaning,
Hero Kyyaz’s countenance changed.
That day Kyyaz thundered,
And flew into a fierce rage.
Not sparing a single soul among the people,
This Kyyaz scattered his wrath,
As though he would swallow them whole.
When his wife gave birth, hero Kyyaz
Roared in fury,
And summoned, without exception, those skilled in cunning,
The mighty and wise, eloquent in counsel,
Calling all his people together,
The elders of the Seven Valleys,
Gathering every last one.
The multitude came in turmoil,
And dear Kutu saw
How dark Kyyaz’s face had grown.
Kutu was the blessed elder of the people,
An eloquent man whose mouth poured forth words,
A healer who revived the fainthearted,
A good man who raised others up,
A renowned master of speech,
An accomplished and capable man.
Kutu came and stood there.
That mighty giant Kara Döö
Had formed a plan that day:
If my father, hero Kutu,
Should fall into an argument with him,
And they should fight until both turned pale,
I will draw my sword from its sheath,
And raise a dreadful tumult.
I will crush them like grain,
Striking high and low,
And without killing the child,
I will wrest him from Kyyaz.
What began in the morning lasted until evening;
His foster father, hero Kutu,
Put Kara Döö between them,
And watched with desperate vigilance.
Kutu lay searching for a way:
If only I could appeal to the Dangyts!
Saying nothing and offering no counsel,
He pondered this in his mind,
Writhing like a white tiger.
Wrapped in his blue coat of mail,
Hero Kyyaz, if you had seen him,
Raged like a blue bear.
Hero Kyyaz stood dumbfounded.
Clutching his thigh and working himself up,
So monstrous was Kyyaz’s arrogance
That the hair on his crown stood on end;
Your lord Kyyaz bristled,
Writhing in frenzy.
Dear Kyyaz himself
Hit upon a devious scheme.
Growling and working himself into a rage,
He cried, “All the countless black Jediger,
Come, let none remain behind!”
Unable to bear his anguish,
Kyyaz conceived evil
Against the child born of the womb,
Against the spring flowing from the ravine;
The madman plotted evil
Against the young hero in chain mail.
His fiery eyes blazed fiercely,
His bloodlust truly seized him,
Strength surged through his body,
And on that dark, ill-fated hour,
Kyyaz, destroyer of nations,
Grew black hair across his face.
His two sunken eyes truly blazed,
And he violently ground
The great teeth in his jaws.
He drew in his throat and clenched himself,
Taking breath with a growl.
The countless black Jediger,
Despairing of their precious lives,
Fled away in frantic haste.
Without speaking many words or uttering a sound,
Hero Kyyaz was struck speechless.
You have called him another man’s son,
Though the young hero came from your own flesh.
It has been eleven months since you took her,
And good fortune and prosperity have settled upon you:
Your wife has borne a son.
Consider the reckoning, hero Kyyaz.
If you destroy your own child,
And in Aichürök’s heart
An unresolved grievance remains,
If dark suspicion lodges in her mind,
May she not put on her swan plumage,
May she not go seeking Khan Akun,
Gathering an army from Akun,
And mustering a mighty host.
When summer comes,
Let us not mount mares with flowing manes;
When autumn comes,
Let us not drive lambs with streaming tails.
Let us not face one another across the slopes,
Clashing and fighting,
And fall into some extraordinary feud!
Let us not load the camels,
Nor, by attacking her child,
My hero, bring some strange torment upon ourselves!
If we attack her child,
If we become needlessly entangled in disaster,
This unfortunate Chürök,
Capable of wondrous upheaval,
Has the strength to gird her waist,
And a place of refuge already secured.
This keen-eyed woman knows a great deal
And commands respect among the people.
Will she not summon those who rule all the earth,
And gather every lord?
Will she not gather every hero
Who boasts of strength and giant stature?
Will she not turn the quarrel bitter?
Sparing not her life, will this woman
Not rise and fight us?
Kara Döö, whose fame reaches across the world,
Stands there grinding his teeth.
The blessed and impartial hero Kutu,
Cried out like a young goose;
Your poor uncle Kutu’s
White beard gleamed.
His counsel was wise, his words were honey;
Once he grieved, no man like him remained.
Speaking gently but with firm resolve,
Dear Kutu began his speech.
Hero Kutu spoke these words,
Saying this to hero Kyyaz:
“My son Kyyaz, you have honor.
Let blessed Kutu speak one word;
Hear it and understand, gray-maned lion.
My son Kyyaz, heed my words!
When God strikes a khan,
He clashes with his wife
And battles with his people.
They grasp spears and bind themselves for war;
He becomes a stranger to his kin
And an enemy to his own nation.
When calamity is about to engulf a khan,
He begrudges each task he gives his servant
And counts every morsel eaten in his house.
Good fortune departs from the khan’s head,
The golden throne vanishes beneath him,
That mountain-like support disappears,
And then, crying out in a little cluster,
His people leave him too!
A good man’s head remains unharmed.
When God is about to strike a khan,
Let alone his people—even the wife in his embrace
Becomes his enemy.
Kyyaz, you were the hero,
And I was the people’s orator.
Your thoughts have become divided:
